title: Given the root of a binary tree, imagine standing on the left side of it; return the values of the nodes visible from the left, ordered top to bottom. This is the first node of each level in a level order traversal.
shortTitle: Left View of a Binary Tree (First Node of Each Level)

s1_definition.profdef: The mirror of the right view. Run Tree BFS with the level-size snapshot and, for each level, record only the first node dequeued (when the index equals `0`). Those first nodes, top to bottom, are the left-side view. Time O(n), space O(w).
s1_definition.analogy: Looking at the National Bank of India approval tree from the left edge, you see only the leftmost approver on each rank, because they stand in front of everyone to their right on that rank. Collecting the leftmost approver per rank top to bottom is the left view.
s1_definition.oneliner: BFS per level; capture the first node of each level into the result.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The mirror of the right view. Run Tree BFS with the level-size snapshot and, for each level, record only the first node dequeued (when the index equals `0`). Those first nodes, top to bottom, are the left-side view. Time O(n), space O(w).

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Looking at the National Bank of India approval tree from the left edge, you see only the leftmost approver on each rank, because they stand in front of everyone to their right on that rank. Collecting the leftmost approver per rank top to bottom is the left view.

**One line to remember:** BFS per level; capture the first node of each level into the result.

sections.s2_technical:
The traversal is the standard BFS with the level-size snapshot, enqueuing children left then right. Inside the drain loop, when the loop index is `0` the node is the first of its level, so add its value to the result. The result becomes the leftmost node per level in top-to-bottom order.

For example a tree with levels [1], [2,3], [4,5] gives left view [1,2,4]. As with the right view, the left view is defined per level, so the first node on a lower level can descend from a right subtree if the left side is shorter; the rule `i == 0` captures it correctly regardless of parentage.

A senior-level nuance is the symmetry with the right view and the common bug: following only left children fails when the right subtree runs deeper. The level-based first-node rule avoids that. An equally valid DFS variant visits left before right and records the first node seen at each new depth, using a depth-indexed result; both are O(n), and the BFS version is often clearer to reason about.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India displays a left-edge summary of its approval tree, showing the first approver on each rank, which represents the entry approver reachable at that depth on the left flank. The display must show the leftmost approver per rank top to bottom, correct even when the right side runs deeper. This is exactly the left view: BFS capturing the first node of each level.

The code contains a `ViewNode`, a `LeftViewService` with `leftView(root)`, and a demo.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: root 1; level 2 is 2,3; level 3 is 4,5 (both under 2).

Step 1: Level 1 has one node. Index 0 so record 1. Enqueue 2,3.

Step 2: Level 2 drains 2 then 3. Index 0 (node 2) is first, record 2; index 1 (node 3) is skipped. Enqueue 4,5.

Step 3: Level 3 drains 4 then 5. Index 0 (node 4) is first, record 4; node 5 skipped.

Step 4: Left view is [1,2,4].

Final output:

```
2026-10-27 19:25:42 [INFO] Left view: [1, 2, 4]
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: tree rooted at 1
    │
    ▼
  LeftViewService.leftView()  (first node per level)
    │ L1 first=1 → [1]
    │ L2 first=2 → [1,2]
    │ L3 first=4 → [1,2,4]
    ▼
  Output: [1, 2, 4]
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The left view of a binary tree is the mirror of the right view: it is the first node of each level, top to bottom, the nodes visible when standing on the left side. I compute it with Tree BFS and the level-size snapshot, recording a node whenever the drain-loop index is zero, which marks the first node of the level, while enqueuing children left then right exactly as in every other Tree BFS variant.

Just as with the right view, the key correctness insight is that this is defined per level, not per branch. Following only left children fails when the right subtree runs deeper than the left, because then the first node on a lower level can descend from a right subtree, and the first-index rule still captures it correctly. I note that a depth-first variant that visits left before right and records the first node seen at each new depth is equally valid and also linear, but the BFS version reads more directly.

In my work at the National Bank of India this produced a left-edge approval summary showing the first approver on each rank, the entry approver reachable at that depth on the left flank, and it had to remain correct even when the right side of the hierarchy ran deeper. Capturing the first node of each level with BFS gave that summary reliably, and presenting the left and right views together as the symmetric first-node and last-node rules is what shows an interviewer I see the whole Tree BFS family as one coherent pattern rather than a set of unrelated tricks.
